text:
maria: Heads-up — we've been seeing repeated churn in the gpu-intermittent nodepool this week. Short-lived pods (cron inference jobs) wake every 3–7m and cause nodes to come up and get immediately drained. Thinking we need an eviction strategy that avoids repeatedly cold-starting GPUs. Thoughts?

junaid: Ack. Noticed the same in eu-west-1. Cold GPU startup ~45s + model load ~30–60s, so user-facing spikes when they hit warm-pool misses.

liam: Can you paste an example pod spec? Are these using nodeSelector/taints?

maria: Example is simple: 
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  labels:
    app: batch-infer
spec:
  tolerations:
  - key: "gpu-intermittent"
    operator: "Exists"
  containers:
  - name: infer
    image: rwd/infer:prod
    resources:
      limits:
        nvidia.com/gpu: 1
```
They don't have PDBs or high priority. They sleep 2–5m, run for 10–20s, exit.

paige: Oof. Frequent node churn is basically paying double — node hours + repeated model init. We should avoid draining nodes that are likely to see another short run.

samir: Quick options: 1) Use a warm-pool with a longer cooldown for intermittent nodepool. 2) Mark nodes with a label like "intermittent=true" and tune Cluster Autoscaler scale-down for that nodepool (disable aggressive scale-down). 3) Use PodPriority + PDBs to reduce eviction for pods that would restart slowly.

junaid: I tried option 2 in a stage cluster: set cluster-autoscaler flag --scale-down-unneeded-time=20m for the intermittent pool. Reduced churn but increased cost 8%. The tradeoff looked acceptable.

liam: Another idea: run a tiny sidecar daemonset that keeps the GPU's driver & model cache alive without consuming the node pool slot. But that still keeps node up. Not ideal.

maria: What about using a special eviction annotation on pods so the autoscaler leaves nodes alone if they host pods with label `keep-warm=yes`? CA supports filter by annotation?

paige: CA doesn't natively support a per-pod protect annotation, but you can add a script to mark nodes as non-scale-down via the cluster-autoscaler's node autoprotect feature (or cordon/annotation). Also we can use the cordon TTL hack: annotate node with `cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/scale-down-disabled=true` and remove after X. Ugly but works.

samir: Prefer a declarative approach: create a short-lived controller that watches pod lifecycle and sets a node annotation `rwd/warm=1` with a TTL when an intermittent pod runs. The autoscaler sees the annotation and skips scale-down. When TTL expires, node becomes eligible.

junaid: +1. We wrote something like that for ephemeral test runners. Pattern: when a GPU-using pod starts, set `rwd/keep-warm-until=<ts>`. CA config: ignore nodes with annotation `rwd/skip-scale-down=true`. Controller flips that annotation on for a node for 12m after last pod exit.

maria: How do we prevent node starvation? If many crons all want to keep nodes up, we could keep all nodes up and pay for them. Need a soft cap and a cost SLO.

liam: Suggest tiered policy: 1) idle threshold: if node <20% GPU utilization for >10m, mark for soft-cooldown. 2) If node has repeated short-lived pods (X runs in Y window), set to warm for longer. 3) Global cap: maintain at most N warm nodes per AZ for intermittent pool; evict beyond cap regardless.

paige: We should factor in spot/preemptible availability. For preemptible, warm nodes mean we can lose them anytime; model load cost remains. Dedicated reserved nodes for warm pool might be cheaper per unit time for predictable workloads. Need cost calc.

maria: Can someone sketch the controller behavior? I can own a PoC. Requirements: minimal permissions, works with CA, TTL logic, respects global warm cap per AZ, exposes metrics.

samir: Pseudocode idea: 
```
on PodStart(p):
  if usesGPU(p) and isIntermittentLabel(p):
    n = getNode(p)
    setNodeAnnot(n, "rwd/keep-warm-until", now+cooldown)
    incrementMetric(warm_nodes[n.az])

on PodExit(p):
  if usesGPU(p):
    schedule check: if no active gpu pods on n then leave annotation until TTL

periodic: prune annotations older than now
enforce cap: if warm_nodes[az] > cap: remove oldest annotations
```
liam: That looks good. For CA integration, we rely on CA ignoring nodes with `rwd/keep-warm-until` or `rwd/skip-scale-down=true`. We'll need a small CA patch or a sidecar that adds `cluster-autoscaler.kubernetes.io/scale-down-disabled=true` to the node.

junaid: Operational notes: metrics to watch — warm_nodes_count, cold_starts_per_hour, avg_model_load_time, cost_delta. Also add alert when cold_starts spiking above baseline.

paige: Also test with max-burst traffic: if we keep warm nodes but then get a big sustained spike, we need autoscaler to bring additional capacity. Ensure controller doesn't block scale-up.

maria: Thanks all — I'll start the PoC for the controller with a 12m default cooldown and a per-AZ cap of 3. I'll open a PR and post the link here when ready. If anyone has objections to 12m or cap=3, speak now.

liam: Fine with those defaults for eu-west-1 initial test.

samir: +1. Let's also add a simple e2e using a synthetic cron to validate cost/latency tradeoffs.

ops-bot: Deployed test cluster `gpu-intermittent-test` created by maria at 1863001248.

maria: Created the repo rwd/gpu-warm-controller and pushed PoC branch `ttl-annotate`. PR in ~2h. :rocket:
